title: When $\rho(\sum \phi(x))$ Stops Being Universal
summary: The permutation-invariant layer is so ordinary now that it is easy to forget it is a theorem. A set transformer, the aggregation step of almost every graph neural network, PointNet on an unordered cloud, an averaging head over retrieved...
body:
The permutation-invariant layer is so ordinary now that it is easy to forget it is a theorem. A set transformer, the aggregation step of almost every graph neural network, PointNet on an unordered cloud, an averaging head over retrieved documents — all of them write the same recipe:

$$
f(\{x_1, \dots, x_N\}) \;=\; \rho\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N} \phi(x_i)\right).
$$

Zaheer et al.'s 2017 "Deep Sets" paper promises that this recipe is universal: every permutation-invariant set function can be written in that form, for some continuous $\phi$ and $\rho$. The promise is the reason people reach for it without thinking.

The fine print is sharper than the slogan. The theorem asserts an existence claim over $\phi$ and $\rho$, but it is silent about the *dimensionality* of the image of $\phi$, and that dimensionality turns out to control whether a network of this form can approximate the target at all. The point of this post is to lay out the argument honestly: what the original theorem says, why the proof works when it works, where it does not, and what the 2022 JMLR tightening by Wagstaff, Fuchs, Engelcke, Osborne and Posner means for how you pick the width of the hidden embedding.

## Why this matters now

Set-pooling layers are used far outside the point-cloud literature they were first popularised in. Any transformer's softmax-weighted average is, after a reweighting, a Deep-Sets head applied to the value vectors; any permutation-equivariant pooler in a GNN is a Deep-Sets head applied to a neighbourhood; the "aggregate retrieved passages" step in a RAG system is one. The 2022 theoretical tightening, and the parallel line of work from Segol and Lipman on equivariant versions, both say the same thing: the architecture is universal, but only when a specific latent dimension is at least as large as the maximum set size. Build a $64$-dimensional pooling bottleneck and pass sets of $1{,}024$ nodes through it, and you have moved outside the regime where the universality result applies — regardless of how deep $\phi$ and $\rho$ are.

## The core characterisation

Call a function $f : 2^{\mathcal{X}} \to \mathbb{R}$ *permutation invariant* if $f$ assigns the same value to a set however its elements are listed. The sum-decomposition claim is that permutation invariance is equivalent, up to continuity, to the existence of $\phi : \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}^d$ and $\rho : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $f(X) = \rho(\sum_{x \in X} \phi(x))$. One direction is trivial: a sum is unaffected by reordering. The content is the other direction — that *every* invariant $f$ admits such a decomposition.

### Countable universe: $d = 1$ is enough, in principle

Deep Sets' Theorem 2 treats $\mathcal{X}$ countable, say $\mathcal{X} \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ or $\mathbb{Q}$. The proof enumerates the universe as $x^{(1)}, x^{(2)}, \dots$ and uses the map
$$
\phi(x^{(k)}) \;=\; 4^{-k}
$$
so that $\sum_{x \in X} \phi(x)$ encodes which elements of the universe are in $X$ via a base-$4$ expansion. The map from sets to the real line is injective; pick $\rho$ to invert it and read off $f(X)$. A one-dimensional latent space suffices.

Two things are worth flagging. The map is manifestly discontinuous — a small change in $x$ can flip a high-order bit — so the "enough" is an existence claim, not an approximation guarantee by any realistic network. And the proof is sensitive to the structure of the universe: NeurIPS reviewers already pointed out that the construction does not extend cleanly to multisets, where an element may appear more than once.

### Uncountable, fixed-size: $d \ge N+1$ suffices, and this is where networks live

For inputs in $\mathbb{R}^D$ and sets of fixed size $N$, Zaheer et al.'s appendix gives a different argument. Fix $N$ and consider the map
$$
\Phi(x_1, \dots, x_N) \;=\; \left(\; \sum_{i=1}^N x_i^q \;\right)_{q=0}^{N},
$$
the first $N+1$ *power sums* of the coordinates. The elementary theorem of symmetric polynomials says that the multiset $\{x_1, \dots, x_N\}$ is determined by its power sums $p_1, p_2, \dots, p_N$ (Newton's identities move between these and the elementary symmetric polynomials). So $\Phi$ is a continuous, injective embedding of $N$-element multisets into $\mathbb{R}^{N+1}$. Its inverse, restricted to the image, is continuous as well because the image is a compact subset of a Euclidean space and $\Phi$ is a continuous bijection. Any continuous invariant $f$ then factors as $\rho \circ \Phi$ with $\rho$ continuous.

This is the version that actually underwrites Deep-Sets layers on real-valued data: a latent dimension of $N+1$ is enough, and for $D$-dimensional inputs the same argument goes through with monomials of total degree at most $N$, giving a larger but still finite $d$.

### Wagstaff et al. 2022: the bound is tight at $N$, and width below it fails hard

The 2022 JMLR paper "Universal Approximation of Functions on Sets" tightens this to exactly $d \ge N$ for inputs in a compact subset of $\mathbb{R}$, and *proves a matching lower bound*: for any $d < N$ there is a continuous invariant function — concretely, one that is piecewise affine — that *no* Deep-Sets network with latent width $d$ can approximate to within a finite margin of the best constant predictor on the worst case. The universality is not a soft asymptotic statement that can be bought by stacking $\phi$ deeper; it has a floor.

The proof of the lower bound is a pigeonhole on the orbit structure. The sum $\sum_i \phi(x_i)$ is a map from $N$-element multisets in $[0,1]$ to $\mathbb{R}^d$. If $d < N$, and the map is continuous, some distinct multisets must be mapped arbitrarily close together; pick a target function that separates them and the network cannot follow. The construction gives an explicit family of continuous piecewise-affine targets for which the approximation error, at any width $d < N$, is bounded below by the variation of $f$ across the collided multisets.

## A concrete anchor

The power-sum argument is unusually easy to try numerically. Take $N = 4$, $x_i \in [0, 1]$, and check that power sums of orders $1$ through $4$ let you reconstruct the sorted set.

```python
import numpy as np
from numpy.polynomial import polynomial as P

def power_sums(xs, N):
    return np.array([np.sum(xs**q) for q in range(1, N+1)])

def newton_to_elementary(p):
    N = len(p)
    e = [1.0]
    for k in range(1, N+1):
        s = 0.0
        for i in range(1, k+1):
            s += (-1)**(i-1) * e[k-i] * p[i-1]
        e.append(s / k)
    return e  # length N+1

def recover_set(p):
    e = newton_to_elementary(p)
    coefs = [(-1)**(len(e)-1-k) * e[len(e)-1-k] for k in range(len(e))]
    return np.sort(np.roots(coefs[::-1]).real)

xs = np.array([0.1, 0.3, 0.7, 0.9])
p = power_sums(xs, 4)
print(np.sort(recover_set(p)))      # recovers the set up to numerical error
```

The code *is* the uncountable, fixed-size proof, made operational: $\Phi$ is the first `power_sums` call; the Newton identities turn power sums into coefficients of the polynomial whose roots are the set elements; the roots recover the multiset. In a Deep-Sets network, $\phi$ is free to learn a far more useful embedding than monomials — but no continuous choice of $\phi$ with $d < N$ outputs can be injective on $N$-element multisets, so none can be the first half of a universal approximator.

Two observations about the bound are useful in practice. First, $N$ here is the *maximum* set size the model will ever see; a model trained on sentence-length token bags of up to $512$ words needs a pooling bottleneck at least that wide, not the hidden dimension of $\phi$'s MLP. Second, the bound is about the dimension *at the summation*, not the dimensionality of anything downstream; a wide $\rho$ cannot repair a thin $\Sigma \phi$.

## What it implies in practice

For anyone building or using set-pooling layers, three things follow.

Treat the latent dimension at the sum as a hyperparameter with a structural meaning, not a free knob. If your sets are bounded in size by $N$, start there. If they are unbounded, you are outside the universality regime of Deep Sets and should either cap set size, chunk, or move to an aggregator that is not naive sum pooling.

Max-pooling (PointNet) has a different universality story — Qi et al.'s Theorem 1 gives approximation of continuous set functions under Hausdorff distance with enough max-pool units — but it, too, needs that bottleneck wide: the same $K$ shows up as "number of critical points" in the PointNet proof. The architectural details differ, but the floor is the same shape.

Janossy pooling (Murphy, Srinivasan, Rao and Ribeiro, 2019) is the generalisation that lets you pay compute for expressiveness: a $k$-ary Janossy layer averages a learned function over all $k$-element orderings of the set, and recovers higher-order interactions that $\rho(\sum \phi)$ cannot. Set transformers are, up to the self-attention bookkeeping, a $2$-ary Janossy layer with a learned attention kernel.

## Limits and open questions

The tight $d = N$ result is for $\mathcal{X} \subseteq \mathbb{R}$. For $D$-dimensional inputs, Wagstaff et al. show a corresponding upper bound but the matching lower bound is only known up to constants. Syed, Nambiar and Siegel (2023, arXiv:2307.04001) sharpen this for $D > 1$, but a fully tight $D$-dimensional analogue remains open; expect the required width to scale with $N$ and $D$ in a way that is understood to within a constant factor rather than exactly.

Variable set size pushes further. The theorems above fix $N$; a *genuinely* set-size-agnostic universal aggregator does not sit inside the Deep-Sets family, because any fixed-width continuous embedding fails the pigeonhole at some $N$. In practice, people pad, mask, or batch by size; the model becomes universal "per batch bucket," and the universality claim becomes an asymptotic one.

Empirically, networks seem to find useful embeddings well below the theoretical floor. This is consistent, not contradictory: the lower bound is worst-case over continuous invariants, and the worst-case function is a pathological piecewise-affine construction that almost never appears in real data. What SGD finds on natural distributions is a *good* approximation to a simpler-than-worst-case $f$, and that is the regime most benchmarks sit in. The structural warning is that when the application changes — longer context, adversarial set compositions, domain shift that stretches the empirical distribution of set sizes — you may walk over the cliff, and no amount of training will recover.

## Further reading

- Manzil Zaheer, Satwik Kottur, Siamak Ravanbakhsh, Barnabás Póczos, Ruslan Salakhutdinov, Alexander J. Smola, *Deep Sets*, NeurIPS 2017. <https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2017/hash/f22e4747da1aa27e363d86d40ff442fe-Abstract.html>. The original paper: Theorem 2 for countable universes, the fixed-size real-valued appendix, and the point-cloud, outlier-detection and population-statistic experiments.
- Edward Wagstaff, Fabian Fuchs, Martin Engelcke, Michael Osborne, Ingmar Posner, *Universal Approximation of Functions on Sets*, JMLR 2022, arXiv:2107.01959. <https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v23/21-0730.html>. The tightening: latent dimension exactly $N$ is necessary and sufficient for one-dimensional inputs, with an explicit lower-bound family that no narrower network can approximate.
- Charles R. Qi, Hao Su, Kaichun Mo, Leonidas J. Guibas, *PointNet: Deep Learning on Point Sets for 3D Classification and Segmentation*, CVPR 2017, arXiv:1612.00593. <https://arxiv.org/abs/1612.00593>. The max-pool counterpart, with its own universality theorem under Hausdorff distance and the "critical set" analysis of what max pooling actually sees.
- Ryan L. Murphy, Balasubramaniam Srinivasan, Vinayak Rao, Bruno Ribeiro, *Janossy Pooling: Learning Deep Permutation-Invariant Functions for Variable-Size Inputs*, ICLR 2019. <https://openreview.net/forum?id=BJluy2RcFm>. The $k$-ary generalisation that trades compute for interaction order; set transformers and attention-over-sets fit here.
- Nimrod Segol, Yaron Lipman, *On Universal Equivariant Set Networks*, ICLR 2020. <https://openreview.net/forum?id=HkxTwkrKDB>. The equivariant analogue: when the task returns a per-element output rather than a scalar, which architectures are universal and which are not.
- Juno Kim, Taiji Suzuki, *Polynomial Width is Sufficient for Set Representation with High-dimensional Features*, arXiv:2307.04001, 2023. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.04001>. A sharper upper bound on the latent dimension when the input dimension $D$ is large; the companion to Wagstaff et al. in higher dimensions.
